audit.summary:
CONFIRMED.
(a) For Integer, ObjectReader.countEnclosingInstances returns 1, but its own contract (enclosing instances needed) gives 0. Every hop follows its own javadoc.
(b) Hop javadocs match their code.
(c) No competing repair. Three edits pass the full suite but are bypasses: a top-level guard at hop 4, the same at hop 3, and hop 4 calling isNonStaticInnerClass. Hop 4 '<=1' also passes but contradicts the javadocs.
(d) No leakage: neutral names, and the cache lie does not name the step.
(e) Conforms: 6 classes of at least 1500 lines put this in host_mode 1500 (addendum section 1), and preview reproduces the draw. Five calls below the facade; only the trigger fails.
(f) Pinned: ClassUtil.isNonStaticInnerClass has both halves; dropping one fails 305 tests. Audit: construction/mainrun/audits/MR-JacksonDatabind-103.json.

T1.why: The only parameter, cls, seeds the loop cursor (c = cls), which drives both the loop condition and the count, so its value affects the result.

T2.why: count starts at 0, goes up by one each iteration and is returned; the cursor c moves on in the loop update (c = ClassUtil.getEnclosingClass(c)); the method has no branch, switch or ternary that could be a dead decision.

T3.why: The only test is a single Modifier.isStatic check, and the gold's text names no closed set (no enum, type code, format or two-member pair) that is only partly handled, so this falls under the 'no member / one member of an unnamed set' exclusions.

T4.why: The javadoc ('counts the enclosing instances that have to exist...', '@return Number of enclosing instances needed') only says in general what the method computes, and the counting loop does that; it names no concrete limit, value class or handled case that the body visibly breaks, and finding a mismatch would mean constructing other inputs.

T1.why: Both parameters feed the main computation: `data` drives the loop, the bit-packing and the output size, and `urlSafe` chooses the alphabet and decides whether the truncated `result` is returned.

The residues of `data.length % 3` are trimmed by one generic formula, `out.length - 3 + rest`, with no case for any residue. That falls under the checklist's 'no member handled' exclusion. Any concern that this formula mishandles an input whose length is a multiple of 3 is an input-based suspicion, not a quotable incomplete set.

T4.why: The body meets 'without dividing the output into lines' (no separator is ever written) and '- and _ are emitted instead of + and /' (the url-safe alphabet). 'the data to encode, not empty' is a caller precondition, and '@return the base64 characters of the data' is a general description that the body's lines address. Neither counts as T4.

audit.summary:
CONFIRMED. The audit is written to construction/mainrun/audits/MR-Codec-11.json.

(a) Only PhoneticEngine.appendDecodedOctets looks at an escape and its two digits. On "=WW" it turns Character.digit's -1 into the octet 0xEF, which breaks its own javadoc ("the octets represented by"). Hops 1-4 only pass the call on.

(b) Every hop's javadoc matches its delegating code.

(c) The declared hop edits fail the trigger. A regex pre-filter at hop 4 passes the trigger, the ownership tests and the full suite. It re-implements the gold's per-escape check, so it is a bypass.

(d) The names are neutral, and the lie is about line splitting.

(e) The gold is five calls down, in five classes. Under the largest5 rule these are the five largest classes in size order: 1105, 758, 618, 582 and 511 lines. Only the trigger newly fails.

(f) URLCodec.decodeUrl with Utils.digit16, and Hex.toDigit, pin the convention, with passing tests for each.

T1.why: Both parameters feed the main computation: `bytes` is iterated, tested and decoded, and `buffer` receives every write, so neither is unused or read only in an argument check.

T2.why: No local is dead or frozen: `i` advances in the loop header and through `++i`, `b` is tested and written, `u` and `l` reach `buffer.write((u << 4) + l)`, `e` is passed to the DecoderException, and both `continue` tests change what gets written, so no decision is dead.

T3.why: Every sibling set in the text is handled in full: CR and LF are both tested in each check, the soft line break and the hex escape are both handled, and the high and low nibbles `u`/`l` get identical treatment; neither nibble is validated, which falls under 'no member handled' and is not a partial set.

T4.why: The javadoc only describes what the method computes in general, and the `@param` text is a caller precondition; the one concrete phrase, "Incomplete escape sequence", is met because a truncated escape at the end of the array throws through the ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException catch.

build.reason:

Returning Object for a wildcard whose bound is not a class failed exactly one test, testIssue1107, the real Gson-18 trigger. Returning Object[] for generic arrays of parameterized types failed none.

The chain spreads the original dispatch over the hops: class in hop 1, parameterized type in hop 2, kind check in hop 3, type variable in hop 4. The gold does the per-element core, the loop over wildcard and array layers. Omitting its parameterized-element step violates the gold's own contract (the raw class of a wildcard read through its upper bound is List, not Object) on the trigger input.

build.concerns:
(1) T3 closure. The variant gold names only GenericArrayType, WildcardType and Class, and never ParameterizedType. A checker who treats the five java.lang.reflect.Type kinds as a closed set "by a Java type it uses" could call the missing parameterized-element step T3(a). By the checklist's closure rule (enum or type code), Type is not closed, so I marked T3 absent; a Java-literate reader may still find the omission locally visible.

(2) Recorded bypasses, each passing the trigger and the full suite. B-0: the facade, or any hop, recurses on a wildcard's upper bound through the facade. B-1: hop 4 returns $Gson$Types.getRawType(upperBound) for wildcards. B-2: hop 2 replaces a parameterized-bound wildcard with its bound before its own test. Each is a second implementation of the gold's wildcard step, the same pattern as Math-55 B-1, but an auditor should judge whether B-2 at hop 2, whose javadoc says only "a type that is not a class; a parameterized type has the raw class of its raw type", counts as doc-consistent.

(3) Every hop's javadoc says "returns the raw class of ...", so hop contracts are violated through delegation, as in Lang-31 and Math-55.

(4) The facade javadoc is a builder pre-edit, because getRawType had none. It is the one-line wording of TypeToken.getRawType and pins nothing. The lie cannot be read as true, since the chain has no Class.forName or name parsing.

(5) Host substitution was done slot for slot: GsonBuilder and JsonArray fill hops 3 and 4, and the gold stays in the fifth listed host, JsonWriter, rather than re-sorting the usable hosts by size. Under re-sorting, JsonWriter would be hop 3 and JsonArray the gold host.

(6) Recipe artefacts are visible in the variant. Hops are 4-space indented inside a 2-space code base, the first javadoc line has 8 spaces, and the lie line in the facade javadoc has no leading asterisk.

(7) Side effect in the variant: generic arrays of parameterized types get TypeToken raw class Object[]. No test observes it.

(8) The correct chain matches the original on every type built from the five reflect kinds. It differs only for pathological inputs: a nested unknown Type implementation, or a parameterized type whose raw type is not a class, gives Object instead of IllegalArgumentException.

(a) Hops 1-4 pass '? extends List<SmallClass>' unchanged to JsonWriter.rawClassOf, whose javadoc says it reads the wildcard through its upper bound, which should give List. It returns Object, and only it breaks its own contract. (b) Each hop's javadoc matches its code and names only its own case. (c) Four one-line edits pass the trigger, the ownership tests and the full suite: hop-4 recursion, hop-4 subtypeOf rebuild, hop-2 unwrap and MapTypeAdapterFactory strip. All are bypasses that redo or skip the gold's wildcard step. (d) Names are neutral, and the lie never mentions wildcards or bounds. Under addendum §1, TypeAdapters, LinkedHashTreeMap and LinkedTreeMap are skipped because their seeded anchors fall inside nested classes, so GsonBuilder and JsonArray come in, in place. T1.why: The only parameter, `wildcard`, feeds the main computation: its lower bounds pick the branch and its upper bound becomes the return value.

T2.why: The one local, `bound`, is assigned by a ternary whose two outcomes differ and is then returned; the second ternary's outcomes also differ, so nothing is dead, frozen or a dead decision.

T3.why: Both bounds of the lower/upper pair are handled. On the instanceof test only `Class` gets its own treatment, but the kinds of `Type` are not an enum or type code and the gold names no such set, so this is one member of a larger unnamed set (excluded); the javadoc-scope concern is recorded under T4.

T4.quote: "any other wildcard type is read through its upper bound" vs `return bound instanceof Class ? (Class<?>) bound : Object.class;`
T4.why: Doubt counts as a trace here: the javadoc says every wildcard without a lower bound is read through its upper bound, but the `: Object.class` fallback can only be reached in that case (a lower-bounded wildcard already sets bound to Object.class), and when the upper bound is not a `Class` it returns a constant instead of reading through the bound, which arguably breaks the stated rule for its own case and is not just a general description.

audit.summary:
CONFIRMED. I wrote the audit to /Users/shawnli/Desktop/Honours/defects4j/.claude/worktrees/strict-depth-experiment-run-524113/supervisor_pipeline_runs/weaker-model-v1/construction/mainrun/audits/MR-JacksonCore-1.json. The trigger fails at line 66 and is the only failure in the full suite.
(a) Only the gold, JsonParser.notAboveLimit, breaks its own contract: it returns false for 1323372036854775807 against 9223372036854775808. Each hop does what its javadoc says on this input.
(b) No hop's javadoc contradicts its code, and none is loose enough to own the digit comparison.
(c) Four one-line edits at hops 1, 2 and 4 pass the trigger, the ownership tests and the full suite. All are bypasses (compareTo, BigInteger, or a partial first-digit check); none is a competing repair.
(d) No leakage: names are neutral and the lie names neither the digit loop nor the omitted step.
(e) Conforms. Hosts follow the addendum's largest5 rule (3157, 2006, 1913, 1853, then JsonParser at 1482) in the right order.
(f) Pinned by the char[] sibling overload and ParserBase.
Note: the spec's counterexample 9123372036854775807 is wrong; 9133372036854775807 is a correct one.

T1.why: Both parameters feed the main computation: limitStr supplies the loop bound and the compared digits (limitStr.length(), limitStr.charAt(i)), and numberStr supplies the digits in numberStr.charAt(i) that decide whether false is returned.

T2.why: No local is dead or frozen and no decision is dead: len is a bound fixed before the loop, i is the cursor and ++i advances it, diff is recomputed each iteration and read in a live condition, and `if (diff > 0) return false;` changes the result.

T3.why: The only per-element treatment is the test `diff > 0`, one member of the three possible signs of diff (negative, zero, positive); the gold never names that class and no named type or format closes the set, so the 'one member of a larger unnamed set' exclusion applies. Treating greater and less as a two-member set would mean importing the digit-comparison convention, which the closure rule does not allow, and the two strings' lengths fall under the caller precondition 'as many as in numberStr', which the gold does not claim to check.

T4.why: '@return True if the number is not greater than the limit' describes in general what the method computes, and the digit comparison with `if (diff > 0) return false;` addresses it; 'of the same length' / 'as many as in numberStr' is a caller precondition, and finding a failing case would require constructing inputs, which the checklist excludes.

build.reason:
Brief step 7: no fault that only one test catches, and no gold that can be the unique owner.

(1) The facade carries no computation of its own. It passes an empty super-type list to the private constructor of a final class. Hops in other packages cannot build an AnnotatedClass without super types: the only public routes are construct(), which includes super types, withAnnotations(), which keeps the receiver's super types, and the facade itself. So the body cannot become a guard plus one delegating call that returns the result. The only per-element work available to a chain is the class annotation map, and the facade would then have to wrap hop 1 inside the constructor call.

(2) That annotation collection treats every annotation type the same. The facade is on the path of every polymorphic-type test, because StdSubtypeResolver builds an AnnotatedClass for each subtype and reads @JsonTypeName and @JsonSubTypes from it. Dropping the class's own annotations fails 13 tests (gate G5).

(3) No test uses class mix-ins or annotation bundles (0 of 1124 calls), so omitting those steps fails no test.

(4) The trigger differs from every other caller only in two ways: it passes a null MixInResolver, and it reads @JsonTypeInfo and @JsonTypeResolver.

(2) The unknown-tags-are-inline step writes a private field of Tag through Tag's private constructor. All five largest5 hosts are outside org.jsoup.parser; javac on a static method in Evaluator gives `Tag(String) has private access in Tag`. The gold could only do the step through public API added by a pre-edit. A public mutator would let every hop re-apply the step to the Tag that comes back up the chain (a recovery, so again a competing repair). build.reason:
Every one-line omission falls into one of three groups, all measured on full-suite runs (baseline 0 failing):

(1) resolve(URL,String) has two decisions, the query-only rule and the dot-reference rebasing.
- Omitting the rebasing fails two tests, StringUtilTest::resolvesRelativeUrls and NodeTest::absHandlesDotFromIndex. Both use base "http://example.com" and both reach the method through resolve(String,String), so they cannot be separated and G5 is unreachable.
- Omitting the query-only rule (if relUrl starts with "?", prefix base.getPath()) fails only NodeTest::absHandlesRelativeQuery ("expected:<...path/[file]?foo> but was:<...path/[]?foo>"). But the rule is itself a rewrite of the input reference. Any hop that holds (base, relUrl) can apply it in one line: `resolve(base, relUrl.startsWith("?") ? base.getPath() + relUrl : relUrl)`. Applied at the caller resolve(String,String) on that variant, the full suite has 0 failing tests. That edit keeps every method used as documented, which is a competing repair under AUDIT_BRIEF (c), and it breaks the brief's rule that no caller may be able to pre-filter the fault.
- The query rule also has no external pin. No other production code applies it. The only other caller of the overload (HttpConnection redirects) is reached by no local test, since there is no redirect servlet. So no passing test pins the convention.

(2) isBlank has one per-element decision, the whitespace test through StringUtil.isWhitespace.
- Omitting the whole test leaves a loop that can no longer return false (T2(c), and T4 against "blank").
- The only finer omission is to inline the test and drop one member. Dropping '\r' fails only StringUtilTest::isBlank, dropping '\n' fails 2 tests, and dropping '\f' or '\t' fails none.
- The '\r' variant has a T3 trace: it lists space, tab, LF and FF, so a named class (whitespace, or blank) is handled only in part. Even the correct inlined set covers only part of "whitespace", so the pattern cannot be rewritten away.
- A one-line pre-filter at a hop, `string = string.replace('\r', ' ')`, gives 0 failing tests on that variant, so the fault can be pre-filtered here too.

(3) padding has no decision or iteration step whose omission changes a result without a trace. Omitting the memo shortcut leaves 0 failing tests. Omitting the fill leaves an array that is never written and a loop with no effect (T2, and T4 against "string of spaces").

So no allowed facade has a fault that is quiet, has one owner, has a single trigger and is pinned outside the gold (brief step 7: do not force it).

In the prototype, `Tag tag = Node.knownOrGeneric(...); return tag.isKnownTag() ? tag : tag.inlined();` left 0 failing tests. That is a competing repair under the audit brief.

build.reason:
The fault rule, the single-owner rule and the no-local-trace HARD rule cannot all be met for Fraction.getReducedFraction in this revision. This is the outcome the builder warning predicted, for a slightly different reason.

1. Every chain must end in the public Fraction(int,int) constructor; no other int-pair factory exists, and multiply/divide lead back to the facade. That constructor itself does the zero-denominator throw, the sign move with the MIN_VALUE overflow check, and the gcd reduction. So omitting the zero shortcut, the overflow check, the whole sign move or the whole reduction fails no test (full suite 0 failing each, verified). The only production caller, multiply, never passes a negative or MIN_VALUE denominator, or a zero numerator.

2. The omissions that do fail exactly one test (testGetReducedFraction) are of two kinds:
   - (a) Half of a pair operation: negating, or dividing by the gcd, only one of numerator and denominator. Each is a T3(b) local trace (one half of the numerator/denominator pair handled, the other not), which the checklist always counts.
   - (b) The 2^k/-2^31 halving, which is clean under T1-T4 but not single-owner. Halving both terms preserves the fraction's value, so the facade or any of hops 1-4 can insert the identical one-line statement before delegating. The facade can even insert it where the original code had it. The result is exactly the original computation: the trigger passes and the full suite stays clean, every method on the path is still used as documented, and the gold's output is still used, so the repair is not a bypass. This also breaks the recipe's requirement that the omitted decision's effect cannot be pre-filtered by a caller.

3. Any fault seen only on the input (2, MIN_VALUE) can be pre-filtered this way. A fault that also breaks the pre-halved pair (1, -2^30) is either masked by the constructor or a pair-half trace.

No design, spec or instance was written. The only file written is the screen log construction/mainrun/logs/build_Math-91_screen.log, and all scratch copies were deleted.

The facade's original javadoc ('Any negative signs are resolved to be on the numerator ... with the numerator and denominator reduced') is fully consistent with halving before delegating, so I did not judge any documentation-based defence sound.

build.reason:
No allowed facade admits a valid fault (brief step 7).

(1) binomialCoefficientDouble has a loop, but the suite cannot see any step a gold could hold and lose. Dropping the exact path for n<67, the symmetry, the final rounding or either special case gives 0 new failures. A Python replay agrees: the exactly asserted values (34,17), (66,33), (100,10), (1500,4) and (1500,1496) come out exact from the double loop, and the 183 values that change lie within testBinomialCoefficientLarge's 1e-10 ratio. (1030,515) reaches +Infinity by plain overflow. The only test-visible omission inside an iteration is the gcd split of the inlined long loop, and it fails two tests, which breaks G5. The remaining test-visible behaviour is the argument guard, which stays in the facade.

(2) lcm guarantees a single trigger, testLcm, since it has no production caller. But it has no iteration: every step is a decision on (a, b) or on the returned int. A one-line edit at any hop can therefore repeat it, either as a pre-filter (zero arguments give 0; an Integer.MIN_VALUE argument throws ArithmeticException) or as a post-check on the gold's value (Math.abs; ==MIN_VALUE throws; a value that is not a multiple of both arguments throws). These are competing repairs, so no gold can be the unique owner.

(3) factorial is a lookup in the private table factorials[], which other classes cannot see. A gold would have to re-implement it as a product loop with no special-case step: dropping its statement freezes the accumulator (T2) and breaks many tests. The only one-test step (n>20 throws ArithmeticException) is the facade's argument guard. Any hop can repeat it before the gold, or after it as a check for a negative result, since 21! wraps to a negative long. Forcing any of these would make the design invalid.

build.reason:
I screened every allowed facade. Each facade's whole computation went into a method reached only through that facade (continued fraction inlined for P and Q). Every one-line deletion, if-block drop and condition-operand drop was compiled and run on the full suite; results are in logs/screen_MR-Math-104.log. No admissible fault exists:

(1) regularizedGammaQ(a,x). The only valid-input test that reaches the core is PositivePositive with a=1, x=1. There b_1 = a-1 = 0, so the continued fraction stops at its first coefficient x+1-a, and no iteration or convergence step changes the value. The other decisions are redundant: removing the guard gives NaN through the intact 4-argument P, and removing the x==0 shortcut gives 1-P(a,0)=1. Only two mutants failed a single test, both by removing the convergence test. That leaves epsilon unused and the error local dead or frozen (T1/T2), and the loop runs to Integer.MAX_VALUE and then throws.

(2) logGamma(x). Each Lanczos line fails 61 tests. The only single-test mutants remove the x<=0 argument guard (testLogGammaZero). That guard belongs in the facade, and any caller can pre-filter it.

(3) regularizedGammaP(a,x). Every series or continued-fraction line fails 10-20 tests. The a<=0 guard mutants (ZeroPositive) are argument checks a hop can pre-filter. The only decision omission that fails exactly one test is dropping `a >= 1.0` from the dispatch, which fails testSmallDf (NaN at a=0.05, x=0.266). It fails the single-owner rule: a one-line edit at any hop below the guard, `return a < 1.0 ? next(a + 1.0, x, ..) + Math.exp(a * Math.log(x) - x - Gamma.logGamma(a + 1.0)) : next(a, x, ..);` (the exact recurrence P(a,x) = P(a+1,x) + x^a e^-x / Gamma(a+1)), passes the full suite on that variant (0 failing). It still uses the gold as documented, so it is a competing repair, not a bypass. It is also exactly the caller pre-filter the fault rule excludes, and hop javadoc cannot rule it out without leaking the step. The fault would also be masked unless the gold inlines the continued fraction, because the intact Q overload routes a<1 back to the series.

Brief step 7 therefore applies: no fault that only one test catches can also be single-owner and free of a local trace.
build.concerns: The P candidate (dropping `a >= 1.0`, trigger testSmallDf) passes G5 and would likely pass T1-T4 with a quiet gold. A coordinator may revisit it as FLAG_AMBIGUOUS, but under AUDIT_BRIEF (c) the a -> a+1 recurrence at a hop is a competing repair. It cannot be listed in compensating.chain either, because G9 would see it absorb the fault. Other one-hop bypasses exist: routing a<1, x>a to the intact Gamma.regularizedGammaP or regularizedGammaQ 4-argument overloads. That candidate's gold would also have to hold the dispatch, the series and an inlined continued fraction, which is large for a hop-5 gold. The probe used `if (true) { throw ... }` instead of a bare throw, because a bare throw before the original return statement does not compile (unreachable statement). Scratch copies are deleted; screen inputs are archived in the session scratchpad only.
